guide.title: Bushwick, Brooklyn: Eleven Breweries in Fourteen Blocks
guide.intro: The Dutch founded Bushwick as Boswijck — heavy woods, or little town in the woods — and Governor Peter Stuyvesant chartered it in 1661. It became part of the City of Brooklyn in 1854. What made the place in the nineteenth century was beer. German immigrants built a brewing district so concentrated that an NYC Parks historical sign counts at least eleven breweries operating within a fourteen-block area, and a second account puts the number at 14 breweries by 1890. Prohibition ended that between 1920 and 1933, and Sicilian families followed the Germans into the neighborhood; by 1950 Bushwick was one of New York City's largest Italian American neighborhoods. Two more turns of population and one catastrophic night have reshaped it since.

sections.heading: Beer, the blackout, and what came after
sections.body:
The brewers left their buildings behind. The William Ulmer Brewery at 31 Belvidere Street, built between 1872 and 1890 in the German round-arch style — the main buildings by the architect Theobald Engelhardt, the stable-storage building by Frederick Wunder — was designated a New York City Landmark on May 10, 2010, the first brewery building in the city to receive that status, and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on February 20, 2024. It closed in 1920 under Prohibition; the complex was adaptively reused rather than demolished and now holds residential and mixed-use space.

The brewers also left a church. St. Barbara's Roman Catholic Church at 138 Bleecker Street, completed in 1910 in the Spanish Baroque Revival style by the architects Helmle and Huberty, was founded as a national parish for German Catholic immigrants; the local brewer Leonard Eppig contributed to it, and the parish's name is tied to his daughter Barbara. Its congregation shifted from German to Italian to Hispanic across the twentieth century, and it remains an active parish under the Diocese of Brooklyn.

Bushwick's population was almost 90% white in 1960 and less than 40% white by 1970, as Puerto Rican and other Caribbean families became the predominant population amid the economic decline that followed the brewery closures. Then came the July 1977 blackout, when Bushwick suffered severe looting and arson damage; the business vacancy rate on Broadway reached 43% afterward, and the damage lingered for years.

Since the 2000s, rent pressure in Manhattan and northern Brooklyn has drawn young professionals and artists into converted warehouse lofts and the existing brownstone and limestone rowhouses. One product of that period is visible from the sidewalk: the Bushwick Collective, founded in 2012 by a neighborhood resident who donated his own wall and then coordinated with other building owners to open more walls to artists. Work by Buff Monster, Phlegm, Blek le Rat and Olek has gone up on those walls, and the collective runs an annual block party.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Bushwick's stations sit on three lines.

On the L, Jefferson Street sits at Jefferson Street and Wyckoff Avenue, DeKalb Avenue and Morgan Avenue are both recorded as being in Bushwick, and Morgan Avenue sits at Morgan Avenue and Harrison Place.

Myrtle-Wyckoff Avenues is served by both the L and the M, and serves Bushwick and Ridgewood, Queens together — Wyckoff Avenue forms the Brooklyn-Queens border at that point.

On the M alone, Central Avenue sits at Myrtle Avenue and Cedar Street and Knickerbocker Avenue at Myrtle and Knickerbocker Avenues, both in Bushwick.

On the elevated BMT Jamaica Line, four stations sit on or near the Bedford-Stuyvesant boundary. Myrtle Avenue, at Myrtle Avenue and Broadway, carries the J, M and Z. Chauncey Street carries the J and Z. Halsey Street carries the J. Gates Avenue is served by the J at all times except peak-direction rush hours and by the Z in the peak direction at rush hours only. Flushing Avenue, further west, is served by the J and M with the Z skipping it; its source places it in Bedford-Stuyvesant while noting that it also serves adjacent parts of Williamsburg and Bushwick.

No NYC Ferry landing is recorded for the neighborhood, and there is no Long Island Rail Road station in Bushwick.

sections.heading: Where to stay
sections.body: No hotel is listed here; the lodging list is left empty rather than reaching into a neighboring neighborhood. The nearest verified lodging is in Williamsburg: the Wythe Hotel at 80 Wythe Avenue, in a converted 1901 brick industrial building, and The William Vale at 111 N 12th St.

faq.question: How do I get to Bushwick?
faq.answer: By subway, and by several. The L calls at Jefferson Street, DeKalb Avenue and Morgan Avenue; the L and M share Myrtle-Wyckoff Avenues; the M alone calls at Central Avenue and Knickerbocker Avenue; and the J, M and Z serve the elevated Jamaica Line stations at Myrtle Avenue, Chauncey Street, Halsey Street, Gates Avenue and Flushing Avenue.

faq.question: Where does the name Bushwick come from?
faq.answer: From the Dutch Boswijck, meaning heavy woods or little town in the woods. Governor Peter Stuyvesant chartered the area under that name in 1661.

faq.question: Is there anything left of the breweries?
faq.answer: Yes. The William Ulmer Brewery complex at 31 Belvidere Street still stands, adaptively reused as residential and mixed-use space; it was the first brewery building in the city designated a New York City Landmark, on May 10, 2010. Green Central Knoll was built on the former site of the Rheingold Brewery.

faq.question: Who was Maria Hernandez?
faq.answer: A local anti-drug activist who was shot in her Starr Street home in August 1989. The City Council renamed the park — opened as Bushwick Park by 1896 — in her honor that year.

faq.question: Where can I see the Bushwick Collective murals?
faq.answer: The collective is centered on Troutman Street and St. Nicholas Avenue, and the murals are on building walls, viewable from the street at any hour. Note that the organization's own website currently carries unrelated injected content and is not a reliable source of information.

faq.question: Is there a hotel in Bushwick?
faq.answer: No hotel is listed here. The nearest verified lodging is in Williamsburg — the Wythe Hotel at 80 Wythe Avenue and The William Vale at 111 N 12th St.

places.name: Maria Hernandez Park
places.address: Irving Ave. and Knickerbocker Ave., between Starr St. and Suydam St., Brooklyn
places.summary: At 6.87 acres, the largest community park in Bushwick, with a circular plaza, a playground, dog runs and sports courts.
places.history: The site was once partially owned by the showman Phineas T. Barnum and his wife Nancy, who hosted circus activities and used it for storage. The City of Brooklyn bought the land from the Barnums and other owners in the early 1890s and had made it a showplace park by 1896, when it opened as Bushwick Park. The City Council renamed it in 1989 for Maria Hernandez, a local anti-drug activist shot in her Starr Street home that August.

places.name: Irving Square Park
places.address: Wilson Ave. and Knickerbocker Ave., between Halsey St. and Weirfield St., Brooklyn
places.summary: A 2.76-acre park filling a full city block, which NYC Parks calls Bushwick's town square. Two projects between 2006 and 2008 renovated the park and playground and added antique-style gates, a performance space and a garden plaza; the children's playground sits near the Knickerbocker Avenue entrance.
places.history: Kings County purchased the parcel from Henry Roth and his wife in 1895 for $70,000. Washington Irving is the likely honoree of the name. The surrounding area had earlier been owned by the Duryea family, descendants of French Huguenot immigrants who settled in Bushwick in the 1680s.

places.name: Green Central Knoll
places.address: Flushing Ave., Central Ave., Noll St., and Evergreen Ave., Brooklyn
places.summary: A 2.74-acre park built on the former home of the Rheingold Brewery, with a softball field and a small children's playground set apart from the field by a decorative rocky path.

places.name: William Ulmer Brewery
places.summary: The former brewery complex, built between 1872 and 1890 in the German round-arch style and now converted to residential and mixed-use space. The buildings still stand and are seen from the street.
places.history: The main buildings are by the architect Theobald Engelhardt and the stable-storage building by Frederick Wunder. The brewery closed in 1920 under Prohibition. The complex was designated a New York City Landmark on May 10, 2010 — the first brewery building in the city to receive that status — and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on February 20, 2024.

places.name: St. Barbara's Roman Catholic Church
places.summary: A Spanish Baroque Revival church completed in 1910 by the architects Helmle and Huberty, founded as a national parish for German Catholic immigrants. It is still an active Roman Catholic parish under the Diocese of Brooklyn.
places.history: The local brewer Leonard Eppig contributed to the parish, whose name is tied to his daughter Barbara. The congregation shifted from German to Italian to Hispanic over the twentieth century.

places.name: The Bushwick Collective
places.address: Centered on Troutman Street and St. Nicholas Avenue, Bushwick, Brooklyn
places.summary: An open-air street-art collective that has turned building walls along Troutman Street and the adjacent blocks into a rotating outdoor gallery. It is free and visible from the sidewalk, and it hosts an annual block party.
places.history: The collective was founded in 2012 by a neighborhood resident who donated his own wall and then coordinated with other building owners to open more walls to artists. Murals by Buff Monster, Phlegm, Blek le Rat and Olek have gone up among them.

places.name: House of Yes
places.address: 2 Wyckoff Avenue, Brooklyn, NY 11237, entrance at 408 Jefferson Street
places.summary: A performance-driven nightclub and event venue. Its own site advertises live shows every Friday and Saturday, and the entrance is around the corner from the Wyckoff Avenue address, at 408 Jefferson Street.

places.name: The Bushwick Starr
places.summary: A nonprofit Off-Off-Broadway theater presenting new and experimental theatrical work, with a current production calendar on its own site.

places.name: Roberta's
places.summary: A wood-fired pizzeria open at its original Moore Street location since January 2008, now the first of several Roberta's locations. Its Moore Street address sits near the line with East Williamsburg and sources differ on which neighborhood label to use; the restaurant's own site gives Bushwick.

Dutch colonists settling eastern Brooklyn in the 1650s formed the towns of Flatbush, Bushwick and New Lots.
The B60 runs the Wyckoff and Bushwick Avenue corridor through Bushwick, and Brownsville is listed among the communities it serves.
The Village of Williamsburgh was incorporated within the Town of Bushwick in 1827 and split off as its own town in 1840.
